title: The Exponential Time Hypothesis, Explained Simply, and Why OpenAI Just Shattered It
author: Niaz Bin Siraj
excerpt: On October 26, 2026, OpenAI announced that its AI system had disproved the Exponential Time Hypothesis. Here is what ETH actually is, why it matters so much, and why this could be the most important breakthrough in theoretical computer science in decades.
contents:
On October 26, 2026, OpenAI officially announced that its AI system had disproved a long-standing belief in computer science called the Exponential Time Hypothesis, or ETH. If this result holds up to peer review, it could reshape the entire field of computing. But before we get to the announcement itself, let us first understand what ETH actually is, why computer scientists have believed in it for decades, and why disproving it is such a massive deal.

What is a "Hard" Problem in Computer Science?

To understand ETH, we first need to talk about what makes a problem "hard" for a computer to solve. Not all problems are equal. Some problems are easy. A computer can solve them quickly, even when the input is large. Other problems are incredibly slow to solve, and the time it takes grows at a terrifying rate as the input gets bigger.

lightbulb
Think of it this way

Imagine sorting a deck of cards vs. trying every possible arrangement of those cards. Sorting is fast, trying every arrangement is impossibly slow. That gap is the heart of computational complexity.

Let us use a simple example. Imagine you have a list of 10 numbers and you want to find the biggest one. A computer just looks at each number once, compares them, and picks the largest. If you give it 1,000 numbers instead of 10, it takes roughly 100 times longer. If you give it 1,000,000 numbers, it takes 100,000 times longer. The time grows in a straight line relative to the input size. We call this linear time. It is fast and manageable.

Now imagine a different kind of problem. You have a lock with a 4-digit code (each digit from 0 to 9). You do not know the code, so you try every possible combination. That is 10,000 combinations (10 x 10 x 10 x 10). If the lock had 5 digits, you would need 100,000 tries. Every single digit you add multiplies the work by 10. With a 20-digit code, you would need 100,000,000,000,000,000,000 attempts. This is exponential growth, and it is the enemy of computation.

How Adding Digits Explodes the Work
4 digits→10,000 tries→5 digits→100,000 tries→20 digits→10^20 tries
Each additional digit multiplies the number of combinations by 10. This is exponential growth.

Polynomial Time vs Exponential Time

Computer scientists group problems into categories based on how much time they need as the input grows. The two most important categories for our discussion are:

Polynomial Time
n, n², n³
Time grows gently. Even n cubed is manageable for most real inputs. These are "fast" problems.
Exponential Time
2ⁿ
Time explodes violently. Even small inputs can take longer than the age of the universe.

Here is a concrete comparison. Suppose a computer can do 1 billion operations per second. Look at what happens as the input size grows:

Input size (n)n² (polynomial)2ⁿ (exponential)
10100 ops (instant)1,024 ops (instant)
20400 ops (instant)~1 million ops (instant)
502,500 ops (instant)~1 quadrillion ops (13 days)
10010,000 ops (instant)~1.27 x 10³⁰ ops (40 billion billion years)

Look at that last row. With a polynomial algorithm, 100 items is trivial. With an exponential algorithm, 100 items would take longer than the universe has existed.

warning
This is not a small difference

This is the difference between "solvable in a split second" and "impossible even if you ran every computer on Earth until the sun burns out." That is why exponential vs polynomial matters so much.

Visualizing the Growth Gap

Let us put the numbers from n=100 into perspective visually. If polynomial time (n squared) is a small step, exponential time (2 to the power of n) is a distance beyond comprehension:

n² = 10,000 operationsInstant
2ⁿ = 1.27 x 10³⁰ operations40 billion billion years

The green bar is so small it is barely visible. The red bar fills the entire space. That is what exponential growth looks like compared to polynomial growth, and we are only at n=100.

The SAT Problem - Where It All Starts

Now let us talk about a specific problem called SAT, short for "Boolean satisfiability." It sounds technical, but the idea is simple.

Definition
Boolean Satisfiability (SAT)

Given a set of true/false switches (variables) and a set of rules (a formula) connecting them, can you find a way to set all the switches so that every rule is satisfied at the same time?

For example, suppose you have three switches: A, B, and C. And you have these rules:

SAT Example - 3 Variables, 3 Rules
Rule 1: A must be TRUE, or B must be TRUE
Rule 2: B must be FALSE, or C must be TRUE
Rule 3: A must be FALSE, or C must be FALSE

Solution: A = TRUE, B = FALSE, C = FALSE
Rule 1 passes (A is true) | Rule 2 passes (B is false) | Rule 3 passes (C is false)

With 3 variables, you can just try all 8 possible combinations (2 x 2 x 2). But look at how fast the combinations grow:

83 VariablesTrivial to check
1,02410 VariablesStill fast
1.27 x 10³⁰100 VariablesMore than atoms in the universe
2 x 10⍳⁰300 VariablesBeyond all comprehension

SAT is one of the most important problems in all of computer science. It was the first problem ever proven to be NP-complete, which means it is at least as hard as every other problem in a large class of difficult problems. If you can solve SAT fast, you can solve all of them fast.

What is the Exponential Time Hypothesis (ETH)?

Now we arrive at ETH itself. The Exponential Time Hypothesis was proposed by Russell Impagliazzo and Ramamohan Paturi in 1999. It makes a very specific claim about a version of SAT called 3-SAT (where each rule has exactly 3 variables).

The Hypothesis
Exponential Time Hypothesis (ETH)

There is no algorithm that can solve 3-SAT in sub-exponential time. The exponential wall is real and unbreakable. No shortcut exists. No clever trick will work.

To be more precise, ETH claims there exists some constant c > 0 such that no algorithm can solve 3-SAT faster than a certain exponential rate. Here is the formal statement:

Time(3-SAT) ≥ 2c·n
Where n = number of variables, and c is some constant greater than 0. You can shrink c, but you can never escape the exponential shape of the curve.

How ETH Differs from P vs NP

You might have heard of the famous "P vs NP" question. It asks whether every problem whose solution can be quickly verified can also be quickly solved. Most computer scientists believe P is not equal to NP, meaning some problems are fundamentally hard to solve even if their solutions are easy to check.

ETH is a stronger assumption than P not equal to NP. Here is why:

Hierarchy of Hardness Beliefs
Level 1 - P != NP
"No polynomial-time algorithm exists for SAT"
You cannot solve SAT in time like n² or n³. This is the most widely believed conjecture in computer science.
Level 2 - ETH (Stronger)
"No sub-exponential algorithm exists for 3-SAT"
You cannot even get to 2 to the power of the square root of n. The exponential growth is unavoidable. ETH does not just say polynomial algorithms are impossible. It says you cannot even get anything meaningfully faster than brute force.
ETH is a much bolder claim. The exponential wall is not just tall, it is thick.

Why Does ETH Matter So Much?

ETH is not just an abstract theory sitting in textbooks. It has deep, practical consequences across many areas of computer science. Over the past two decades, hundreds of research papers have used ETH as a foundation to prove that other problems cannot be solved faster than certain known speeds.

27Years StandingSince 1999
1000+Papers Built on ETHLower bounds, hardness proofs
4Major Fields AffectedAlgorithms, graphs, crypto, optimization

1. Algorithm Design

Many algorithms we use today were designed with the assumption that ETH is true. If a researcher proves that "Problem X cannot be solved faster than some speed, assuming ETH," then other researchers stop trying to find faster algorithms for that problem. ETH acts as a guide that tells the community where to spend their effort and where not to bother.

2. Graph Problems

Problems on graphs, things like finding the largest group of friends who all know each other (clique problem), coloring a map so no two neighbors share the same color (graph coloring), or finding the shortest route that visits every city exactly once (traveling salesman), all have lower bounds that depend on ETH.

Problems That Depend on ETH
ETH→Clique→Graph Coloring→Traveling Salesman→Vertex Cover→Set Cover
ETH is the foundation. If it falls, the proven lower bounds for all these problems collapse with it.

3. Cryptography

Much of modern security depends on certain problems being hard to solve. If problems that were believed to require exponential time can actually be solved faster, some cryptographic systems might be weaker than we thought. This does not mean all encryption breaks overnight, but it opens up new questions about the foundations of security.

4. Optimization and Scheduling

Real-world problems like scheduling airline crews, optimizing delivery routes, allocating resources in data centers, and planning factory production lines are all connected to NP-hard problems. ETH tells us that exact solutions to these problems at large scale are fundamentally out of reach, which is why we use approximation algorithms and heuristics instead.

key
The Bottom Line

If ETH is true, these problems genuinely require exponential time, and the best we can do is approximate. If ETH is false, there might be faster exact solutions hiding out there for all of them.

A Real-World Analogy

Think of ETH like a speed limit sign on a highway. The sign says "You can never go faster than 60 km/h on this road." For 27 years, every engineer has designed cars, planned routes, and built infrastructure based on that speed limit. City planners built entire systems around the assumption that this speed limit is real and permanent.

Before (ETH believed true)
60 km/h
Speed limit assumed permanent. Everything designed around this constraint.
After (ETH disproved)
600 km/h
The road can handle much more. Cars, routes, and infrastructure can all be rethought.

Now imagine someone proves the speed limit sign was wrong. The road can actually handle 600 km/h. Everything changes. The cars need to be redesigned. The routes need to be replanned. The entire infrastructure can be rethought. Old problems that seemed impossible because of the speed limit suddenly become solvable. That is what disproving ETH means for computer science.

What OpenAI Announced on October 26, 2026

On October 26, 2026, OpenAI publicly announced that its AI system had produced a formal mathematical proof disproving the Exponential Time Hypothesis. According to their announcement, the AI discovered a novel algorithmic approach that solves 3-SAT in sub-exponential time, directly contradicting what ETH claims is impossible.

auto_awesome
What the AI Found

The AI system reportedly discovered an algorithm that solves 3-SAT in time significantly faster than any known exponential algorithm. If verified, this means the "exponential wall" that ETH described has a door through it.

This is not the first time AI has contributed to mathematics. In recent years, AI systems have helped discover new patterns, verify complex proofs, and suggest new conjectures. But this is fundamentally different in scale and impact. Disproving ETH does not just solve one problem. It pulls the foundation out from under thousands of results that were built on top of it.

gavel
Peer Review is Critical

The result still needs to go through rigorous peer review. The mathematical community is careful, and extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence. A proof of this magnitude will be scrutinized by the best minds in the field. But if it holds up, the consequences are enormous.

What Changes If ETH is Truly Disproved?

If ETH is truly disproved, the effects ripple outward in every direction:

Impact 1
Thousands of "Tight" Lower Bounds Collapse
Algorithms that were considered optimal might not be. Thousands of proven lower bounds that relied on ETH would no longer hold, meaning faster algorithms could exist for problems we thought were already solved as well as they could be.
Impact 2
Practical Computing Could Transform
Problems in logistics, drug discovery, financial modeling, network design, and artificial intelligence that currently require approximations might become exactly solvable.
Impact 3
P vs NP Gets New Momentum
While disproving ETH does not directly resolve P vs NP, it significantly changes the landscape of evidence. The strongest reason many researchers believed P is not equal to NP was that even sub-exponential algorithms seemed impossible. If that assumption falls, the case for P not equal to NP weakens.
Impact 4
Cryptography Faces New Scrutiny
Security researchers will need to re-examine which hardness assumptions still hold and which might be at risk. Systems built on the assumption that certain problems are exponentially hard may need re-evaluation.

AI as a Mathematician

Perhaps equally significant is what this tells us about AI itself. An AI system did not just crunch numbers or search through possibilities. It constructed a novel mathematical proof, a creative act that requires understanding deep structure, making non-obvious connections, and reasoning at a level that was historically considered uniquely human.

Human mathematicians: 27 years, no proof found

AI system: Found a proof in a fraction of that time
This raises a profound question: if AI can disprove a hypothesis that the best human mathematicians could not crack for 27 years, what else can it do?

The boundary between "problems that require human insight" and "problems AI can handle" just shifted dramatically.

Key Takeaways

  1. ETH was a foundational belief. For 27 years, the Exponential Time Hypothesis told us that certain problems would always require exponential time. Thousands of research results were built on this assumption.
  2. The practical impact is real. ETH was not just theory. It shaped how we design algorithms, build security systems, and approach optimization problems in the real world. Disproving it opens the door to faster solutions for problems that affect everyday life.
  3. Peer review is the next step. The result is extraordinary, and it must survive rigorous scrutiny from the global mathematics and computer science community before we can call it settled.
  4. AI just changed the game. An AI system achieving what human mathematicians could not for nearly three decades is a landmark moment. It suggests that AI-assisted mathematical research is not just a nice idea for the future. It is happening now.
  5. This could be a generational breakthrough. If confirmed, the disproof of ETH sits alongside the greatest results in the history of theoretical computer science. It does not just answer one question. It reopens thousands.

We are living through a moment that future textbooks will reference. The Exponential Time Hypothesis stood as one of the strongest walls in computational complexity theory. On October 26, 2026, an AI found a door through it. Now we wait for the mathematicians to confirm whether that door is real.
